text:
On the evening of April 13, 1970, some 200,000 miles from home, three men were settling in for what was meant to be a routine television broadcast. Apollo 13 had left Cape Kennedy two days earlier, carrying Commander Jim Lovell, Command Module Pilot Jack Swigert, and Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise. Their goal was the Fra Mauro highlands of the Moon. They would never get there.

The mission had already known small troubles. Ken Mattingly, the original command module pilot, had been pulled from the crew days before launch after exposure to German measles; Swigert, his backup, stepped in. Then, shortly after liftoff, the center engine of the Saturn V's second stage shut down early. The remaining engines burned longer to make up the difference, and the spacecraft reached orbit. Few people thought much of it. Apollo missions had become, in the public mind, almost ordinary. Television networks had even declined to carry the crew's earlier broadcasts.

The trouble that mattered had been set in motion years before. The spacecraft's service module carried two oxygen tanks, each fitted with a heater, a pair of stirring fans, and a thermostat. Contractors had upgraded the electrical system from 28 to 65 volts, but the thermostat switches in the tank were never changed to match. Before launch, during a ground test, technicians had trouble draining oxygen from Tank 2. To empty it, they ran its heater for hours. The overheated switches fused shut, and nobody knew. The tank's insulation was damaged, though no one could see it.

At about 9:07 p.m. Houston time on April 13, flight controller Sy Liebergot asked the crew to stir the cryogenic tanks, a routine step. Swigert flipped the switch. Within moments, an electrical arc inside Tank 2 ignited the Teflon insulation on the wiring. Pressure climbed. The tank ruptured.

Aboard the spacecraft, there was a bang, a shudder, and a flurry of alarms. Swigert reported the now-famous line, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell, more precisely, repeated it as "Houston, we've had a problem." At first, no one understood how bad things were. Lovell, glancing out a window, saw gas venting into space. He told Houston. Oxygen, the thing that fed both their fuel cells and their breathing air, was leaking away into the dark.

Within minutes, the pressure in the remaining tank began to fall. The fuel cells, which made the spacecraft's electricity and its water, were starving. The Odyssey command module was dying. Mission Control, led that night by flight director Gene Kranz, faced a decision with no precedent. The Moon landing was gone. The question now was whether the men could be brought home alive.

The answer lay in the lunar module, Aquarius. It was a flimsy, spidery craft, designed to support two men for two days on the Moon. Now it would have to sustain three men for four days, in space, on the long road back. The crew powered up Aquarius and shut Odyssey down to save its batteries for reentry. Lovell, Haise, and Swigert crowded into the lander, and they used it as a lifeboat. Nobody had ever planned for it, though engineers had briefly studied the idea years earlier.

The problems stacked up quickly. First came the route. The spacecraft was on a path that would loop around the Moon and, without correction, miss the Earth by a wide margin. Controllers considered a direct abort, but that required the damaged service module's main engine. They chose instead to swing around the Moon and use Aquarius's descent engine to speed the return. A burn about two hours after passing the Moon's far side cut the trip time and aimed the craft at the Pacific.

Then came power. Aquarius had to run on a small supply of battery power and a limited amount of water for cooling its electronics. Controllers asked the crew to shut off nearly everything: the guidance computer was largely idle, the heaters were off, and the lights were dim. The cabin temperature fell toward freezing. Water condensed on the walls. The men slept little, and Haise developed a fever and a kidney infection. They drank very little water to stretch the supply.

Then came the air. Aquarius had enough oxygen, but its lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrubbed carbon dioxide from the cabin, were meant for two men. Three were breathing, and the gas level crept upward. Odyssey had spare canisters, but they were square, and Aquarius's scrubbers took round ones. On the ground, engineers at Houston gathered the odds and ends the crew had aboard: plastic bags, cardboard from flight manuals, duct tape, a spacesuit hose. Within hours, they had designed an adapter. They read the instructions up to the crew, step by step. Lovell, Swigert, and Haise built it. The carbon dioxide level dropped. The device, later nicknamed the mailbox, worked.

Meanwhile, Ken Mattingly, the man who had been grounded, worked in a simulator on the ground. His task was to devise a way to restart Odyssey from a cold, powered-down state using far less electricity than normal. The procedure had never been written, because no one had ever imagined needing it. He and the engineers worked through the night, testing sequences until the numbers closed.

On the third day, a smaller course correction was needed, and it was done by hand. The guidance platform was off to save power, so Lovell lined up the craft using the Earth's terminator, the line between day and night, as a visual reference. He held it steady while Haise fired the engine. It worked.

On April 17, the crew prepared to come home. They jettisoned the damaged service module, and for the first time saw what had happened. One whole panel was gone, blown off. Lovell described a ruined, scorched side of the spacecraft. The images told everyone the explosion had been worse than they feared. Then the men moved back into Odyssey, which was cold, damp, and dark, and powered it up. The procedure Mattingly's team had devised held. Aquarius was cast loose, having done its work.

Reentry brought a final wait. The heat shield's condition was unknown, and the normal communications blackout lasted longer than expected, longer than the three minutes that the engineers had planned. In Houston, controllers watched a silent screen. Fourteen seconds past the expected time, then more. Capcom Joe Kerwin called repeatedly. Then, finally, Swigert's voice came through.

Odyssey's parachutes opened. The capsule splashed down in the South Pacific near the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima at about 12:07 p.m. Houston time on April 17, 1970. All three men were alive. They were tired, dehydrated, and cold. Haise was ill. Lovell had lost fourteen pounds.

The investigation that followed, led by Edgar Cortright, traced the failure to the thermostat switches and the damaged wiring in Tank 2. NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks, removed the stirring fans' hazardous wiring, and added a third tank, separate from the others. The Apollo program continued; Apollo 14 flew the following year.

Apollo 13 is often called a successful failure, and the phrase fits. The mission never reached the Moon. But the way it ended showed what trained people could do together, in real time, under a pressure that few have known. Hundreds of engineers on the ground and three men in a cold, crowded craft solved problem after problem that no manual had foreseen. They brought everyone home.
